progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C01 (Brønsted-Lowry acid and base; HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻; NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ with "only some ammonia molecules do this at any moment"; H⁺(aq) means H₃O⁺). C02 (acid names and formulas, including acetic acid as the acid in vinegar; metals with acids make hydrogen gas). C03 named "strong acids" once. Module 5: dynamic equilibrium and the double arrow (chem-m5-c01, chem-m5-c05). Year 11 Module 2: concentration in mol/L. Stage 5: the pH scale (below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic). Year 11 Module 2: ionic solids dissolving into ions. Not assumed: pH = −log[H⁺], Ka, conjugate pairs.
progression.startsWith: Compare particles in two acid or base solutions. The video opens: Here are two beakers of acid, hydrochloric acid and acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. Both labels say zero point one zero moles per litre, so each litre has the same amount of acid dissolved. But a pH meter reads one point zero for the hydrochloric acid, and two point nine for the acetic acid.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining strong and weak as complete and partial ionisation (or dissociation) with a particle picture; explaining why a weak acid reaches equilibrium with most molecules whole; choosing → or ⇌ for an acid or base in water; naming the common strong acids and strong bases; explaining concentration as amount per litre and drawing the four combinations; explaining why a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong acid, and why strength must be compared at equal concentration using pH; explaining why low solubility is not weakness. No pH calculation (chem-m6-c07), no Ka (chem-m6-c10), no conjugate pairs (chem-m6-c06), no conductivity method or practical procedure (chem-m6-p03, chem-m6-p04).
progression.nextLesson: measuring the pH of a range of acids and bases (route chem-m6-p03).

teaching.task: Two acids, both 0.10 moles per litre: one reads pH 1.0, the other pH 2.9. If they have the same amount of acid dissolved, why is one so much more acidic, and how is a "strong" acid different from a "concentrated" one?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) two acids at the same concentration give different pH and fizz: why? (1); (2) the particle view: every HCl has given its proton to water; only about one acetic acid molecule in eighty has; hydronium makes a solution acidic (2); (3) that is strength: strong ionises completely, weak partly; lower pH means more hydronium, one pH unit is ten times, so about eighty times more (3); (4) a weak acid stops early because the reverse reaction runs too: dynamic equilibrium with most molecules whole; chloride almost never takes a proton back (4); (5) so the arrow: single for complete, double for partial (5); (6) which acids are strong; HF is weak (6); (7) concentration is amount per litre, a separate dial; dilute strong is still strong; four combinations as particle grids (7); (8) a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong one, so compare strength at the same concentration; weak is not safe (8); (9) bases: strong hydroxides dissociate completely; ammonia is weak; same-concentration pH 13 against 11; Ca(OH)₂ and Ba(OH)₂ give two OH⁻ (9); (10) limewater: little dissolves, but all that dissolves splits up: low solubility, not weakness (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two acids at the same concentration read pH 1.0 and 2.9, and particle lenses inside the two beakers show why: every HCl molecule has given its proton to water, only about one acetic acid molecule in eighty has. Strength is then separated from concentration as two dials, a concentrated weak acid is shown beating a dilute strong one, and bases and low solubility follow the same reasoning. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here are two beakers of acid, hydrochloric acid and acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. Both labels say zero point one zero moles per litre, so each litre has the same amount of acid dissolved. But a pH meter reads one point zero for the hydrochloric acid, and two point nine for the acetic acid. Drop in magnesium, and the hydrochloric acid fizzes hard while the acetic acid barely bubbles. Same amount of acid, so why such a difference?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitrous acid (HNO₂) solutions each have a concentration of 0.10 mol/L at 25 °C. The nitric acid solution has a pH of 1.0 and the nitrous acid solution has a pH of 2.2. Explain the difference in pH. Include an ionic equation for each acid reacting with water, using the correct arrow." New pair of acids (the video works HCl and acetic acid); the near-identical formulas test classification. Crossed mistake: "HNO₂ is more dilute". (A2) "A 0.10 mol/L ammonia solution has a pH of 11.1. A 0.0010 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution has a pH of 11.0. A student claims that ammonia and sodium hydroxide are equally strong bases, because their pH values are almost the same. Assess this claim." Bases at different concentrations (the video's concentration surprise uses acids). Crossed mistake: "same pH, same strength".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct an investigation to demonstrate the use of pH to indicate the differences between the strength of acids and bases (ACSCH102)" "construct models and/or animations to communicate the differences between strong, weak, concentrated and dilute acids and bases (ACSCH099)" this video starts with the route's particle comparison (two 0.10 mol/L acids, one lens each) and stops at telling extent of ionisation apart from amount per litre and reading both from pH data. It teaches: strong and weak as complete against partial ionisation (or dissociation, for ionic hydroxides); why a weak acid stops early (a dynamic equilibrium, Module 5 callback); the single against double arrow; the strong-acid list and the strong-base group; concentration as a separate quantity; the four combinations as an animated particle model (the C6-IQ2-05 "model and/or animation"); why a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong one, so strength must be compared at equal concentration (the logic of the C6-IQ2-03 investigation); solubility against strength for calcium hydroxide. pH is used as a meter reading only: lower means more hydronium, one unit is a factor of ten. Not here: pH = −log[H⁺] and any pH calculation (chem-m6-c07); conducting the pH investigation (chem-m6-p03 measures a range; chem-m6-p04 tests strength through pH); conductivity as evidence (named in the out-of-scope list; p04 and c14); conjugate pairs and why chloride never takes its proton back (chem-m6-c06: scene 4 states it as an observation only, and c06 explains it); Ka and pKa (chem-m6-c10); weak-acid ICE tables (chem-m6-c08); salt hydrolysis (the site's L06 card 4; left for the equivalence-point videos, see Open decisions); the HF bond-enthalpy explanation (a crossed chip only).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C01 and C03): the proton is a small teal token; a hydronium ion is a teal token on a pale blue water; a whole acid molecule has an amber outline; anions grey; hydroxide violet; water pale blue; spent labels grey. Board layout (constant): the short question top-left in one line; the main zone holds the lenses, plates or the equation strip, one group at a time; a small amber pH readout chip sits by each solution it belongs to. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items at once; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 19 Oct): `m6-beaker-v1.png` (two copies, coded labels "hydrochloric acid, 0.10 mol/L" and "acetic acid, 0.10 mol/L"; also sodium hydroxide in 9), `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (bench meter with a blank green screen and a probe in a beaker of clear liquid; a coded amber readout sits in the screen), `m5x-strong-acid-mg-v1.png` and `m5x-weak-acid-mg-v1.png` (magnesium ribbon fizzing hard against a few bubbles; hook), `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (hook, small, for "the acid in vinegar"), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (scene 9, coded label "ammonia solution, 0.10 mol/L"), `m5x-saturated-beaker-v1.png` (clear solution over undissolved white solid; scene 10 with coded label "limewater: saturated Ca(OH)₂"). Not used: `m6-limewater-clear-v1.png` and `m6-limewater-milky-v1.png` (a delivery tube bubbling gas into a test tube: they read as the carbon dioxide test, not as a saturated solution); `m6-conductivity-meter-titration-v1.png` (conductivity is out of scope here). No new plates needed. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: Two beakers with pH chips open; a lens zooms into each to show the protons given away; the arrow strip writes single then double; the strong list writes as a card; the four-combination particle grids build one at a time; the base beakers and the limewater lens reuse the same layout; the memory aid writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
